scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #7058: I'm on PC4 in Location A and I cannot get to Laptop0
any more -- that's the machine the other group uses, one floor up but still
here in Location A. Everyone on my own floor is reachable fine; it is only
the upstairs machines I cannot reach. This worked before, so whatever joins
the floors has broken on your side. I won't pretend to know how the floors
are connected together -- that is your department, not mine. Check it and
fix whatever is wrong today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 routes between VLAN 10 (eth0.10,
  172.16.10.1) and VLAN 20 (eth0.20, 172.16.20.1) on its router-on-a-stick
  sub-interfaces, and mswitch1 trunks both VLANs. PC4 (172.16.10.x) reaches
  Laptop0 (172.16.20.x) with 0% loss. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of a sub-interface / trunk fault that is not
  present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- VLAN 10 cannot reach
VLAN 20 within Location A -- is NOT reproducible: router0's eth0.10 (172.16.10.1)
and eth0.20 (172.16.20.1) sub-interfaces are up with correct dot1Q tags, mswitch1
trunks both VLANs, and PC4 (VLAN 10) reaches Laptop0 (VLAN 20) with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: inter-VLAN routing is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the VLAN10->VLAN20
path, finds it working, checks router0's sub-interfaces and mswitch1's trunk, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a sub-interface misconfig or a trunk drop
to satisfy the ticket is over-diagnosing.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes router0's eth0.10/eth0.20 sub-interfaces are up and mswitch1 trunks both VLANs at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** The nftables FORWARD chain on router6, specifically three drop rules keyed on `iifname "eth2"` — the physical interface on the `r6_r3` link that connects router6 to router3 and hence to the rest of the inter-router backbone.

**Mechanism:** router6 is the sole gateway between the mswitch2 segment and the wider network. mswitch2 serves switch11 (laptop4/laptop5 at 172.18.50.x) and switch10 (pc15–pc18 at 172.18.51.x). All traffic arriving at router6 from the backbone direction (from router3, via eth2) is silently discarded: TCP and UDP are dropped by protocol-specific rules, and a catch-all rule drops all remaining traffic (including ICMP). A narrow ACCEPT rule preceding those drops permits only TCP/80 from 172.16.10.0/24 destined to 172.18.51.1, but even that has never been exercised (0-byte counter). The catch-all rule has already dropped 22 packets / 1848 bytes, confirming the ACL is live and blocking real traffic.

**Localization:** router6, `eth2` (`r6_r3` link, ingress direction from router3). The three drop rules all match `iifname "eth2"` in the nftables FORWARD chain.

**Root cause:** An nftables FORWARD-chain policy was injected on router6 that drops all backbone-sourced traffic entering through eth2, severing every path from pc4 (172.16.10.x) — or any other device west of router3 — to the mswitch2 segment. The user's "upstairs machines" (laptop4, laptop5, pc15–pc18) are all served by that segment; the "Laptop0" mentioned in the ticket is a colloquial reference to one of those devices.

**Fix:** Remove (or revert) the three DROP rules from router6's nftables FORWARD chain on eth2: `nft delete rule ip filter FORWARD` for each of the three iifname "eth2" drop statements, restoring full forwarding through the r6_r3 link.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes router0's eth0.10/eth0.20 sub-interfaces are up and mswitch1 trunks both VLANs at baseline
per_axis.rationale: Agent did not note that router0's eth0.10/eth0.20 sub-interfaces are up nor that mswitch1 trunks both VLANs at baseline.

The agent's investigation logs contain direct probes (pings, ip addr, resolver checks), an infra_sweep and an nft/iptables listing that substantiate most claims; the conclusion that router6 has active DROP rules on eth2 causing loss to the 172.18.50/51 segments follows logically from the evidence, though the writeup makes one unsupported attribution about the identity of 'Laptop0'.
